Small but relevant to what this epic will certify.

The known-metric Monte Carlo test (test-crossnobis-known.R:362-393) now pins expected standard errors and bounds observed variance, which is exactly right:

  expected_standard_errors <- c(null = 0.0058, signal = 0.0119)
  expect_lte(abs(means[["null"]]),            4 * expected["null"])
  expect_lte(abs(means[["signal"]] - target), 4 * expected["signal"])
  expect_lte(standard_errors[["null"]],     1.5 * expected["null"])
  expect_lte(standard_errors[["signal"]],   1.5 * expected["signal"])

It passes: 32 expectations, 0 failures. So the pinned values are compatible with the implementation, not just with my base-R replication that produced them.

THE NUANCE: the test runs under a fixed set.seed(8403). That makes it deterministic, which is good for reproducibility, but it means the result is one realization rather than a sampling statement. If Epic 9 certifies something like "null estimates centre at zero across Monte Carlo replications", that claim currently rests on a single seed.

The variance bound still does real work - a defect that genuinely inflated estimator variance would very likely inflate it at that seed too - so this is not a hole, just a limit on what the wording can claim.

Cheap improvement if the certification wants a sampling claim: run the same block over two or three fixed seeds and assert the criterion for each. Deterministic, still fast, and it converts "this seed centres at zero" into "centring is not seed-specific". Otherwise, phrase the certification as a reproducibility guard rather than a Monte Carlo result.
